name: Microsoft
summary: Microsoft's careers site says interviewers look at how you think, not only what you know, and that some roles add coding exercises, portfolio reviews or presentations. Candidates commonly report a loop that mixes coding, design and behavioral questions, often ending with an 'as appropriate' interview, and Microsoft suggests answering with its STAR(R) model: situation, task, action, result and reflection.
rounds: Loop of 3–4 interviews mixing coding, design and behavioral questions
Final 'as appropriate' interview with a senior leader
looks_for: Growth mindset: learning from mistakes and feedback
Customer obsession: using customers' perspectives to shape your work
One Microsoft: collaborating across differences and supporting others' success

questions.text: Tell me about a time you got critical feedback. What did you change?
covers: The feedback, stated plainly, and your honest first reaction
What you changed and how you checked it was working
The reflection: what it taught you about how you learn

questions.text: Describe a time you learned something new quickly to deliver a project.
covers: What you didn't know and how little time you had
How you learned it: docs, small experiments, asking people who knew
What you delivered, and what you'd do differently next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with a team that disagreed on the approach.
covers: The options on the table and who backed which
How you helped the team decide: data, a prototype, agreed criteria
The outcome, and how the team worked together afterwards

questions.text: Design a parking-lot system. Where would you start?
covers: Clarifying questions: size, vehicle types, payment, entry and exit gates
The main objects and how they relate: levels, spots, tickets, payments
Edge cases: a full lot, a lost ticket, many gates updating at once

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped another team succeed, even though it wasn't your goal.
covers: What the other team needed and why it mattered to the wider organisation
What you gave up or took on to help
The result for them, and what it did for the working relationship

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made at work or in a project. What did you do next?
covers: A real mistake, owned in the first person
How you fixed the damage and who you told
What you now do differently because of it

questions.text: How would you design a file-sync service that keeps a user's files up to date across their devices?
covers: Splitting files into chunks and uploading only what changed
Handling conflicts when two devices edit the same file offline
The metadata service, storage and change notifications, and how they scale

questions.text: Explain the difference between a process and a thread, and when you'd use each.
covers: Separate memory for processes, shared memory for threads in one process
The costs: creation, context switching, communication and safety
An example, such as separate processes for isolation and threads for parallel work

questions.text: Users say an app became slow after the latest release. How would you investigate?
covers: Reproducing it and comparing against the previous release
Profiling and telemetry to find where the time now goes
Rolling back or switching the change off if users are badly hit, then fixing the cause

questions.text: What happens when you type a web address into a browser and press Enter? Go as deep as you can.
covers: DNS lookup, then a TCP connection and TLS handshake
The HTTP request, the server's work and the response
How the browser parses, fetches extra resources and renders the page

questions.text: How would you improve online meetings for a team spread across very different time zones?
covers: The real pain points: little overlap, missed decisions, meeting fatigue
Ideas such as recordings with summaries, async updates or smarter scheduling, prioritised
A success metric and a guardrail, such as privacy or meeting length

questions.text: Why Microsoft, and which of its products or teams interests you most?
covers: A specific product or team and the customers it serves
A link to something you've built, used or studied
What you want to learn there

questions.text: How do you keep learning outside work or study, and what are you learning right now?
covers: A specific thing you're learning and why you chose it
How you learn: courses, side projects, reading, mentors
Something you've already applied from it

questions.text: What would you like to know about the team or the role?
covers: Two or three questions about the team's work, customers or challenges
A question about how success is measured in the first months
Questions that show you researched the team, not only the company

tips: Show how you learn: what you tried, what failed, what you'd do now.
Expect a design question even in coding rounds; clarify requirements first.
Use Microsoft's STAR(R) model for stories: situation, task, action, result, and a reflection on what you learned.
Microsoft's own interview tips ask you to start with clarifying questions, state your assumptions and explain your approach out loud.
Match your examples to the job description, and keep one ready about how you handled feedback.
